newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia investment boom sounds 1997 rebound.
newsitem.headline: Australia investment boom sounds 1997 rebound.

text.p: Australian business investment is booming and should ensure economic growth accelerates in 1997 after a modest slowdown this year, said analysts.

Capital expenditure figures for the September quarter suggested investment would even outstrip the government's budget forecast of 14 percent for the 1996/97 financial year, a prediction which had been considered overly optimistic by many.
"This was a crucial result," said Tony Meer, an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "Investment had to maintain the momentum built up in 1995/96 and, however you cut it, it has."
"In fact, it even suggests Treasury may have been a little conservative with their forecast, and who would have thought that a week ago?" he said.
The largely unexpected strength in investment diminished the chances of another easing in official interest rates but did not completely rule out a move during the first quarter of 1997.

"The thing is, the growth in investment is mostly in sectors which are not employment intensive, like telecoms and mining," said Meer. "So if you have concerns about jobs growth, like the RBA has, there may be a case for another rate cut to boost the sectors that are, like retail."
The figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed private new capital expenditure (CAPEX) rose 0.9 percent in the September quarter, seasonally adjusted, on the quarter before.
This was a robust result given that CAPEX had jumped 13.2 percent in the June quarter and well above market forecasts which had centred on a 3.0 percent fall.
Analysts were particularly surprised by a 2.4 percent rise in plant and equipment spending, which did not seem to gell with imports of capital goods which fell sharply in the period.
This alone was likely to add about 0.15 percentage point to Gross Domestic Product growth for the quarter, they said.
"It's positive that the surprise was in plant and equipment spending," said Shane Oliver, chief econmist at AMP.
"It suggests you're probably going to see a positive contribution to growth from business investment."
Equally important was the latest survey of investment intentions for the whole 1996/97 year which showed industry was even more upbeat than the government.

The fourth forecast for 1996/97 -- the ABS takes six surveys in all starting in the December quarter of the previous fiscal year -- was for spending of A$42.91 billion, a 19.2 percent rise on the fourth estimate for 1995/96.

Assuming expectations turn into actual investment at the average ratio of the past five years, the forecast points to spending of A$44.20 billion in 1996/97. That would be a rise of 15.3 percent on the A$38.34 billion recorded for 95/96, which itself represented an annual increase of 11.7 percent.
It boded well for the economy since investment made up about 15 percent of GDP and a result anywhere close to expectations would add about 2.0 percentage points to growth in 1996/97.
"The surprising strength in the expectations for 1996/97 is underpinning the good growth story," said Matthew Drennan, an economist at Axiom Funds Management.
Analysts reckoned the government's budget time forecast of 3.5 percent GDP growth in 1996/97 now looked a lot more reasonable than it had just a month ago.
It would also be a relief to the Reserve Bank which had called investment the "linchpin of forecast growth."
"That means the RBA will be much more comfortable about the fact the rate easings they've done to date have underpinned confidence for the business community," said Drennan.
"The bottom line is that continued investment is supportive of pulling the economy out of the current flat spot."
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
